# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

insights.line: What would make it worth more?

whys.g1: Eleanor's and my answer are both about trying a pair in our own setting before buying, Walter's and Ruth's are both about keeping up with many voices at once, and the two left alone (Diego on cost, Tomas on his one-sided workaround) do not belong in either group; the names are plain.
whys.g2: Tomas's answer is the only off-topic one, since it describes his current workaround rather than what would make it worth more, and it was kept out of the groups.

founder.order_why: Screen 14 (who else has to agree) belongs right after screen 10 (who decides and pays), but it sits after the cost and price screens, so I answered the buyer question, moved on to money, then got pulled back to it.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 10 and 14: 'would the deaf or hard-of-hearing adult decide and pay, or someone else' and 'besides them, who has to agree' ask the same buyer question, and screens 15 and 16 then check and re-choose the same buyer_payer_alignment again.
founder.missing: There was no way to give the price as a one-off hardware purchase plus an optional subscription. AirCaps is $599 glasses, free captions, and $20/month Pro, and I had to force that into one yearly range. There was also no question about HSA/FSA eligibility as a payment route, which matters for whether my buyers can afford it.

PRIMARY.missing: Nobody asked what I actually do today when a conversation gets too fast or noisy (lipreading, asking people to repeat, a captioning app on my phone, just nodding along), where it happens most (restaurants, group dinners, work meetings), or whether the glasses would work with my hearing aids and keep up in a noisy room.

screens.why4: A free box for up to two roles plus the single 'I'm not sure' chip covers every answer, including mine ('Nobody'), with no overlapping or odd option.
screens.why5: My 'Nobody' stands as typed, and the screen adds no role I never named, such as an audiologist or a family member.
screens.why7: The card's founder side is met: a role list of at most two rows of up to 4 words, 'Nobody' allowed so it becomes the fixed Nobody else, and 'I'm not sure' as the only escape, which leaves the dimension out.

screens.why1: Right after I said nobody else has to agree, Keel shows me the list it built from that so I can check it before it goes to strangers.
screens.why2: Short plain rows in my own words, deaf or hard-of-hearing adult and nobody else, readable at a glance, though the intro repeats the title.
screens.why3: Who decides and who pays for a $599 pair of glasses is something I know cold from my HSA/FSA buyers and testimonials.
screens.why4: The same person shows up on two rows, once as having the problem and once as deciding to buy, where one row tagged with both would do, so two rows overlap.
screens.why5: It still says what I picked: the wearer decides and pays, nobody else has to agree, and Keel added no role I never named.
screens.why7: The card says the person with the problem and the decider share one row when they are the same person, and a Nobody else list is a statement to confirm, so splitting the wearer into two rows bends one rule; the belief itself is still Nobody else, as I said.
screens.instead: Nobody else · Deaf or hard-of-hearing adult · has the problem and decides to buy, confirmed as: The deaf or hard-of-hearing adult decides, and nobody else has to agree.

screens.why1: Right after I said nobody else has to agree, Keel shows me the single belief it will test and lets me confirm it or go back, which is what this step is for.
screens.why2: The belief and the title read cleanly, but the bar's 'paid for something for this' needs a second read, and 'decides, and nobody else must agree first' is a stiff way of saying 'decides alone'.
screens.why3: Whether my wearers buy the glasses themselves is something I know from my own customers, HSA/FSA and free returns included.
screens.why4: A list holding only Nobody else is properly turned into a statement to confirm, with a way back to name a role, so nothing is missing or doubled.
screens.why5: I picked Nobody else and the belief says the wearer decides and nobody else must agree, so it means exactly what I gave.
screens.why7: With Nobody else tested, the belief matches my list, and the bar counts only deciding alone as support, so the stranger answers can both support and refute it as the card requires.
screens.instead: Keel will test: deaf and hard-of-hearing adults decide on their own. Holds if at least 2 in 3 say they decided alone the last time they paid for something to help them follow conversations.

screens.why1: After the price and who decides, asking what first step I want a deaf or hard-of-hearing adult to actually take is the obvious next question in 'will they pay'.
screens.why2: The question asks two things at once (the step, and what it costs them), and the hint's examples 'pay for a pilot' and 'let us run a trial' are business-sales words, not how anyone buying caption glasses for themselves talks.
screens.why3: I know exactly what I want a new wearer to do first, which is order a pair on the 15-day risk-free returns, so I can answer from my own business.
screens.why4: The only chip is 'I'm not sure', which the card allows on the founder's side to leave the dimension out, and it fits here.
screens.why5: My typed step 'order the caption glasses with free returns' stands as I wrote it, product named and free returns kept, and nothing is rewritten on this screen.
screens.why7: The screen asks for one step of at most 9 words, says where the money goes, and promises a smaller free step on the next screen when the step costs money; my 7-word step keeps 'free returns' and names the glasses, so the belief 'Most deaf and hard-of-hearing adults would order the caption glasses with free returns' can be tested.
screens.instead: What's the first real step you'd want them to take? (One step, up to 9 words, e.g. "order a pair with free returns" or "try the free app first"; say if it costs them money.)

screens.why1: Right after I named ordering as the first real step, it makes sense to check how strangers will hear that step and the softer yes beside it.
screens.why2: The four answers read cleanly, but the smaller-step line on my Check says 'Yes, after try the caption glasses in person first', which is broken grammar, a 'Yes,' prefix glued onto what should be a short noun phrase, and I had to read it twice.
screens.why3: Whether a deaf or hard-of-hearing adult would order $599 glasses with a 15-day return window is a question my wearers can answer from their own life.
screens.why4: The four answers are complete, distinct and in order: a firm yes to my step, a soft yes, probably not and no, with no escape, as this item requires.
screens.why5: My step is kept word for word, but 'in person' is Keel's addition; I sell online with free returns and have no shops, so 'trying the caption glasses in person' promises a try-on most people can't get from me.
screens.why7: The measure, the count, the order and the 2-for, 2-against balance are all met, the first yes is my own step whole, and the soft yes is a different, free step; but the smaller step shown on the Check is not the noun phrase the card asks for, and it adds an 'in person' condition I never wrote.
screens.instead: Keep 'order the caption glasses with free returns' and make the smaller step 'a video demo of the caption glasses', so strangers see: Yes, I'd order the caption glasses with free returns · Probably, after seeing a video demo of the caption glasses first · Probably not · No.

screens.why1: Right after I set the first real step (order with free returns), asking whether to invite people to take it before the study goes out is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: 'Pilot' is plain to me as a founder, and the hint shows the exact line respondents will see and where I'll find the yeses.
screens.why3: Whether I want early wearers to follow up with is a call I make about my own launch.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it; the two options are distinct and no escape is needed for a founder's own setting.
screens.why5: My step was 'order the caption glasses with free returns', but the respondent's line is a generic 'Would you try this for real? Leave your email', so the commitment I typed is softened into just leaving an email.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? People who say yes see: "Would you order the caption glasses, with 15-day free returns? Leave your email." (Yes, ask them / No pilot)

screens.why1: Picking the interviewer belongs at the end of the flow, but for my respondents, who are deaf and hard of hearing, the voice is the least important thing, and the screen never asks whether a spoken video interviewer suits them at all.
screens.why2: The question, the two names, the 5 s samples and the 400 credits are all plain to me on first reading.
screens.why3: I can judge which voice sounds better, but a sound clip can't tell me which face is easier for my people to lipread or how the captions look, which is what actually matters to them.
screens.why4: The two voices are distinct, but the option many of my respondents would want is missing: text only, or a captions-first interview with no voice.
screens.why5: It uses my own wording, deaf or hard-of-hearing adults, and nothing of AirCaps or my roles leaks to the respondent.
screens.instead: How should Keel ask deaf or hard-of-hearing adults your questions? Daphne on video with captions (watch 5 s) / Saskia on video with captions (watch 5 s) / Text only, no video

screens.why1: Choosing how the study reaches my respondents belongs right after choosing who asks the questions, just before it goes out.
screens.why2: The three choices are plain words; 'AI interviewer' and 'read and tap' are clear to me on first reading.
screens.why3: I know my users well: many lipread poorly on video and most live in text and captions, so I can answer this from what I know.
screens.why4: The options are distinct and the true answer (Read and tap) is there, but the Daphne option leads with 'asks each question aloud' to a deaf audience and nothing offers ASL, so it reads a little odd for my people.
screens.why5: It names my users as I typed them, deaf or hard-of-hearing adults, and nothing of AirCaps leaks into the respondent's options.
screens.instead: How should deaf or hard-of-hearing adults answer? Read and tap (type or speak into boxes) / Daphne on video with every question captioned on screen / Let them choose

screens.why1: After choosing how people answer, deciding who receives the interview link is the natural last step before sending.
screens.why2: Two options are plain, but 'From a search on the Contacts page' names a page I never met in this flow, so I would read it twice to know what list it means.
screens.why3: I know exactly who I would send this to: hard-of-hearing people from our TranscribeGlass days and our waitlist, by name.
screens.why4: Named people, a Keel-found list, and one open link for a deaf and hard-of-hearing group or forum cover the real ways I would reach people, and none of them overlap.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product or roles leaks here, and my pick of people I know by name is offered as written.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? People I know by name (one link each) / People Keel finds for me (a list, one link each) / A group I'm part of (one open link I post there)

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up' sits right under the title with the deciding number beside it (1 of 7 lose 12 or more conversations a month, against a bar of 5 of 7 on the card), though the Price result of 0 of 7 at $599 is the harder fact for my launch and is not the one named.
screens.why_b2: The tally (5 beliefs: 2 holding, 2 not holding, 1 not reached, over 7 people) and each card's count against 'bar 5 of 7' read on first look; only the card numbering jumping from 4 to 6 and the terse 'nothing to ask' made me pause.
screens.why_b3: Price as '$599 up front, then an optional $20 a month plan' and Nobody else agreeing are mine, but I estimated the existing sacrifice as $200 to $1,500 a year in money, and the screen shows it as 'about 12 conversations a month', a recount I recognise but did not type.
screens.why_b4: 'They lose less today than you estimated' and 'they value it below your price' tell me what failed, but not what to try next, such as the price people did name, or whether to aim at the heaviest group-conversation users.
screens.why_b5: Seven people stays visible but is never called small, and 'Commitment: Holding up, 6 of 7 said yes' stands unqualified beside 0 of 7 valuing it at $599, which reads stronger than a free-returns yes can carry.
screens.instead: Not holding up on money: none of 7 would pay $599 (the prices they named are on the Price card), and most lose fewer than 12 conversations a month. 6 of 7 would still order with free returns, so test a lower entry price with your heaviest group-conversation users. Seven people is a small sample.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up, smaller than you think' sits right beside its deciding count, 1 of 7 at 12 or more against a bar of 5 of 7, and the two agree.
screens.why_b2: The strip shows 7 people and marks the bar at 5, but its unit 'conversations of the conversations they are in a month' forces a count through a share frame, so I had to read twice to see it counts conversations per person.
screens.why_b3: It is my Existing sacrifice and my 12 conversations a month, but 'lose about 12 conversations a month: conversations they lost the thread of' says lose twice, and the 'per person' I would expect is gone.
screens.why_b4: The So line restates the count and hands me on to the Price card; it does not say whether to lower my estimate, re-ask in hours, or lean on something other than lost conversations to justify $599.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is visible and flagged as a lean, but the item asked how many conversations 'fell through', not how many they lost the thread of, so 'they lose less than you estimated' leans on answers to a slightly different question.
screens.instead: Ask 'Last month, about how many conversations did you lose the thread of?', label the strip 'conversations per person last month', and say: 6 of 7 lost fewer than your 12, mostly 2 to 8, so a lean says your estimate is high; try about 4 to 8 a month before you build the price case on it.

screens.why_b1: The verdict says 'Not holding up, they value it below your price up front', with 0 of 7 at $599 or more and 0 of 7 at $20 or more against a bar of 5 of 7 right beside it, so I know it failed and by how much.
screens.why_b2: Each ladder shows its bands with counts, marks my $599 and $20 as band low edges, and has its own strip of 7 against with the marker at 5, so what is counted, over whom, and where the bar sits are plain at once.
screens.why_b3: '$599 up front, then an optional $20 a month plan' is exactly my glasses-plus-Pro pricing, under my product's name and my wearers, and it keeps the word optional.
screens.why_b4: The So line tells me where they cluster ($250 to under $599, 6 of 7), which hints at a price point, but then just points to the Insights tab instead of naming the clear pattern in the quotes: try a pair in my own hard situation before paying.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is visible throughout and the small group is called 'a lean, not a call'; the only softness is 'Fewer than 2 in 3' for what is in fact 0 of 7, which understates rather than overclaims.
screens.instead: None of the 7 would pay $599 up front (6 of 7 put it at $250 to under $599), and four said they'd want to try a pair in their own hard situation first: lead with the 15-day free-returns trial, or test a price under $599.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Not reached' sits right beside its deciding number, '0 of 7 named your price or more', and the two agree.
screens.why_b2: The chart's three bars are all zero and the strip draws 5 ghost cells while 7 people answered, so I need a second look to see that the 5 is the floor and not the people.
screens.why_b3: My $599 up front and $20 a month are on it, but the line about money they already spend is Keel's derived belief, which I never checked, and the card doesn't say so.
screens.why_b4: The So line only says the card waits for 5 people at my price; it doesn't point me to the real issue, which is my price sitting above what all 7 named on the Price card.
screens.why_b5: It claims nothing from zero people asked, keeps n=7 visible and says plainly that the card decides nothing.
screens.instead: Not reached: none of the 7 named $599 or more, so nobody was asked where the money would come from. Fix the price first (see Price); this belief is untested, not failed.

screens.why_b1: The card says Holding up with 6 of 7 decided alone beside the bar of 5 of 7, so I know the verdict and the number behind it.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts who had to agree last time they paid, over 7 people, with the bar marked at 5 of 7 on the strip; all three are plain at first look.
screens.why_b3: It's my Buyer and payer belief with Nobody else picked, and the wearer decides alone; 'nobody else must agree first' reads a touch stiff next to the bar line's 'has to agree', but it's my belief.
screens.why_b4: The So line just restates the count; it doesn't tell me to sell straight to the wearer, or remind me that with Price and Ability to pay not holding, who decides isn't my problem.
screens.why_b5: The count line correctly calls it a lean from a small group, but the So line's bare 'They decide alone on purchases like this' generalises past the 6 of 7 who did.
screens.instead: 6 of 7 paid on their own and 1 needed someone else's agreement, so sell to the wearer directly; but with your price not holding, who signs off matters less than whether they'd pay at all.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits beside 6 of 7 said yes and the bar of 5 of 7, so the verdict and the number that decides it are together and agree.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four answers, 7 people show in the strip as 6 for and 1 against, and the marker at 5 shows the bar plainly.
screens.why_b3: The belief is my own step, order the caption glasses with free returns; the only flaws are the doubled Asked: and the rule line's 'after try' where it should say 'after trying'.
screens.why_b4: 'Book them into it' is a vague verb for a purchase, and it does not tell me what to do when the Price card says none of the same 7 values the glasses at $599.
screens.why_b5: It names the small group as 'a lean, not a call', but 'Book them into it' treats a free-returns yes asked without any price as a real order, while every one of the same people valued the glasses below $599.
screens.instead: 6 of 7 would order with free returns, but the question named no price and none of them valued the glasses at $599; this is a lean from 7 people, so ask the six to order at $599 before counting it as a sale.

screens.why_b1: The box says Price is not holding up, and the deciding numbers sit right beside it: 0 of 7 at $599 up front, 0 of 7 at $20 a month, against a bar of 5 of 7.
screens.why_b3: The dimension is Price and the belief line is the one I checked: $599 up front, then an optional $20 a month plan.
screens.why_b4: The group names hint at moves (a demo or loaner pair, better multi-speaker pickup), but the screen never says what this means for the idea, such as whether to lead with the 15-day returns or test a lower entry price.
screens.why_b5: The n stays visible (7 against, 6 asked here, Amaka never saw it), each group shows its count of 2, and nothing claims more than six answers can carry.
screens.why_b6: Two things I hadn't typed: people want to borrow a pair in their own setting before ordering even though I offer 15-day free returns, and the value ceiling is crosstalk (audience questions, eleven people at a family lunch) rather than single-speaker captions; Diego's 'I spend nothing, I lip-read and laugh late' also shows the free-alternative anchor.

screens.why1: As the first screen it plainly checks whether I'm one of the people this is for, before asking anything else.
screens.why2: "Hearing people" is how I and every deaf person I know say it, and the question is short and clear on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know exactly whether I talk with hearing people in a week: at work, the shops, my family, so yes, I can answer this straight off.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it for a weekly-habit question, and there's no need for anything else.
screens.why5: It matches the segment's own words and nothing of a product or company leaks through to me.
screens.why6: One short question with a yes-or-no answer is easy to hold when heard once.
screens.instead: Do you talk face to face with hearing people every week? Yes; No

screens.why1: Right after I said I talk with hearing people every week, showing me the idea makes sense before asking what I think of it.
screens.why2: Live captions, glasses, lens and eye contact are all words I use every day as someone who lip-reads and relies on captions.
screens.why3: Losing eye contact while I look down at a phone transcript is exactly what happens to me at the dinner table or the counter, so I can judge this from my own life.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: It is shown on purpose as an idea, and it stays on what I'd see and do, not on the company's plans or labels for me.
screens.why6: It says well enough, but it repeats 'lightweight glasses' and 'inside the lens' twice in a row, and 'when the people nearby are talking, you wear' sounds like you only put them on mid-sentence, so the middle line is a mouthful heard once.
screens.instead: Imagine AirCaps, an app on lightweight glasses that shows live captions inside the lens. You wear them, and what the people near you say shows up as words in front of your eyes. The people building it believe it would let you read the words while keeping eye contact.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the gate about talking with hearing people, asking how often it went wrong for me last month is the obvious next thing.
screens.why2: Fell through makes me think of plans that got cancelled, not a chat I couldn't keep up with, so I'd have to read it twice to work out what you mean.
screens.why3: I know some conversations last month got away from me, but I never count them, so any number I give is a rough guess.
screens.why4: A box for the number, None for zero and I can't recall for when I don't know covers every answer I could give.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product leaks, but fell through drifts from what was actually lost, which was being able to follow and join in.
screens.why6: The question is short, but A number of conversations last month is a clumsy line to hear aloud, and fell through is unclear by ear.
screens.why7: The box is on the founder's count, period and month, so it could go either way and keeps the one escape, but it uses fell through, the vague verb the card warns against, instead of naming what I saw go.
screens.instead: Last month, about how many conversations with hearing people could you not follow? [ box ] conversations last month · None · I can't recall

screens.why1: Asking what captioning glasses would be worth makes sense right after the AirCaps card, but it sits under a 'What you do today' heading and comes straight after counting conversations that fell through, so it feels a bit sudden.
screens.why2: 'Up front' and 'a month' are how I already think about hearing aids and caption app subscriptions, so I can answer on first read.
screens.why3: I've priced hearing aids and paid for caption apps, so I know what something that lets me follow a table conversation would be worth to me.
screens.why4: Both ladders run from low to high with no gaps or overlaps, 'I wouldn't pay for this' is there as a real answer, and 'I can't say' fits as the way out.
screens.why5: The $599 edge reads like a shop's sticker price rather than a round number I'd think in, so I can guess what they plan to charge.
screens.why6: Each step is one short question with four options and then two, which is easy to hold; the escape is said once and last.
screens.why7: Every rung is money on one measure (an up-front sum, then a monthly sum), one band edge sits at the founder's price on each ladder with two bands below plus 'wouldn't pay' against and three bands for, and 'I can't say' is the one escape.
screens.instead: Same two questions and ladders, but under a heading like 'The idea' rather than 'What you do today'.

screens.why1: Right after I named a price, asking what would make it worth more to me follows naturally.
screens.why2: It reads my answer back the way I would say it, about 250 to 600 dollars up front, and asks one plain thing.
screens.why3: I know what would make captions worth more to me: keeping up in a noisy room, at work or at the theatre, so I can answer from my own life.
screens.why4: It is a box to type in with no options.
screens.why5: AirCaps was already shown on the idea card, so naming it here leaks nothing new and keeps the founder's meaning.
screens.why6: Two short sentences with one question, and the dollar range says well aloud as 250 to 600 dollars.

screens.why1: Asking who had to agree after asking what AirCaps is worth to me makes sense, but the counter jumps from 2 of 5 to 4 of 5, so it feels like I skipped something.
screens.why2: Plain words I'd use; I know right away whether my husband, my insurance or Voc Rehab had a say when I bought my hearing aids or a captioning app.
screens.why3: I've paid for hearing aids, a captioning phone and apps myself, so I can say from my own life who had to agree.
screens.why4: The four run from me alone to someone else deciding, they don't overlap, and 'It was someone else's call' covers the times insurance or Voc Rehab decided for me.
screens.why5: Nothing of the company's plan or its words for people reaches me here; it just asks about my last purchase.
screens.why6: It's short and easy to hold, but the voice says 'You decided on your own' while the screen says 'I decided on my own', so what I hear doesn't match what I read on the caption card.
screens.why7: Nobody else is tested: the four past-tense answers run in order from alone to someone else's call, only 'I decided on my own' counts for it, three count against, and the one escape 'I can't say' is there.
screens.instead: The last time you paid for a hearing aid, captioning app or similar, did anyone else have to agree? I decided on my own · Someone else had to agree · Several people had to agree · It was someone else's call · I can't say

screens.why1: After asking what AirCaps would be worth to me and who'd have to agree, asking whether I'd actually order a pair is the obvious last question.
screens.why2: Caption glasses, free returns and trying them in person are all words I'd use myself, and I got it on the first read.
screens.why3: I buy my own hearing gear and know whether I'd order something like this with free returns, so I can answer from my own life.
screens.why4: There are two yeses and two noes, and trying a pair in person at a shop or demo is a different thing from ordering with free returns, so nothing overlaps and my real answer is there.
screens.why5: It's the AirCaps glasses from the card, with free returns kept, and nothing of the company's plan or its own terms for people like me leaks through.
screens.why6: It's one question with four short options that can be held after one hearing, and there are no symbols or brackets.
screens.why7: The first yes is the step itself and the soft yes is a free smaller step (trying in person, not the free returns again), with two answers for and two against and no escape, as the card requires.
